title: Sublinear testing of bounded-degree graph isomorphism
formal:
Can isomorphism between two arbitrary bounded-degree graphs be tested with a sublinear number of adjacency-list queries? Precisely, does there exist a uniform randomized tester \(A\), with explicit inputs \(n\ge1\), a degree bound \(d\ge1\), and an integer \(q\ge2\), satisfying the following guarantees for every pair of allowed \(n\)-vertex input graphs \(G_1,G_2\)?
\[G_1\cong G_2\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ accepts}]\ge2/3,\]
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)\ge1/q\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[A\text{ rejects}]\ge2/3.\]
For each fixed \(d,q\), its worst-case query bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) must satisfy
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{Q(n,d,q)}n=0.\]
Both graphs are given only through oracles. The graph model, distance and query accounting are specified below. The target retains the sublinear-existence question in the saved card, which is one part of the source’s broader request to determine the full query complexity.
why: The problem asks whether two large sparse structures can be compared without reading a linear fraction of their neighborhoods. It isolates the information needed to recognize structural similarity when both objects are unknown. A resolution would locate a basic boundary of sublinear access and explain whether large connected components create an obstruction beyond the known distribution-like examples.

importance.reason: Tests the fundamental power of sublinear access to compare two sparse graphs without reading the entire input.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

sentences: The tester sees two sparse graphs only by asking for individual neighbors.
It must accept isomorphic graphs and reject pairs that require many edge edits after every possible relabelling.
The question asks for fewer than a linear number of queries at every fixed degree bound and proximity.
Both graphs are unknown, and arbitrary disconnected or highly connected inputs must be covered.
Known small-component testers and recent results for typical known targets do not establish this general two-input guarantee.

definitions:
The graphs \(G_i=([n],E_i)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), are undirected and simple, with maximum degree at most \(d\). Disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. There is no expansion, hyperfiniteness, component-size or randomness promise on their structure.

Graph \(G_i\) is represented by an incidence oracle \(g_i:[n]\times[d]\to[n]\cup\{\bot\}\). Its first \(\deg_{G_i}(v)\) entries at vertex \(v\) list the distinct neighbors of \(v\) in an arbitrary fixed order, and the remaining entries are \(\bot\). The oracles are promised consistent with undirected simple graphs. One adjacency query chooses \(i\in\{1,2\}\), \(v\in[n]\), and \(j\in[d]\), and receives \(g_i(v,j)\). Queries may depend on earlier answers. Correctness must hold for every permitted neighbor ordering.

For a permutation \(\sigma\) of \([n]\), put \(\sigma(E_2)=\{\{\sigma(u),\sigma(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E_2\}\). Define
\[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{iso}}(G_1,G_2)=\frac1{dn}\min_{\sigma\in S_n}|E_1\mathbin{\triangle}\sigma(E_2)|,\]
where \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference. Each deleted or added undirected edge counts once. Thus distance zero means graph isomorphism, and the rejection promise means at least \(dn/q\) edge edits are needed after the best vertex relabelling. Neighbor-list positions do not affect this distance. For nonisomorphic pairs at distance strictly below \(1/q\), either output is allowed.

The tester is a probabilistic oracle Turing algorithm given binary \(n,d,q\), access to both incidence oracles, independent fair random bits and a primitive returning an independent uniformly sampled vertex label in \([n]\). Count every incidence-oracle call and every such vertex-sampling call as one query. All other finite local computation is unrestricted, and the tester must halt. The bound \(Q(n,d,q)\) holds on every allowed pair, every representation and every sequence of random outcomes. Success probabilities include all internal randomness and vertex samples. No graph-dependent advice or full description of either graph is provided; any preprocessing uses only \(n,d,q\).

The degree and reciprocal proximity are fixed when taking the sublinear limit. There is no requirement for one bound uniform in growing \(d\) or \(q\), and no polynomial runtime requirement beyond the query guarantee. Using reciprocal integer accuracies covers all fixed positive proximities by choosing a smaller reciprocal threshold. The edge-edit normalization follows the saved card; the source also uses a convention with a factor of two in the edge threshold. That constant rescaling does not change the all-fixed-proximities existence question.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a tester with the stated correctness, access and sublinear-query guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation of that existence statement. A positive answer must cover every pair of bounded-degree input graphs and every fixed proximity, with two-sided error at most \(1/3\). A near-linear bound that is not \(o(n)\), a guarantee for almost all graphs, a known-target tester, or a result only for small connected components is insufficient. A lower bound of order \(n^{2/3}\) up to logarithmic factors alone does not rule out sublinear testing.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 2.4 explicitly separates testing against a known fixed graph from testing a pair of oracle inputs. This card chooses the latter, as in its saved formulation, and retains two-sided error.

Goldreich proves upper and lower query bounds of order \(n^{2/3}\), up to polylogarithmic factors and proximity dependence, when connected components have polylogarithmic size. The lower bound also applies to general inputs, but the upper bound retains its component-size restriction.

Goldreich and Tauber obtain a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt n)\) tester for almost all fixed regular target graphs, with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Their model supplies the target graph in advance; it neither supplies both graphs only by oracle nor covers every possible target.

The relevant resource here is query complexity. A tester may perform extensive finite computation on its observations. Therefore a fast algorithm for explicit graph isomorphism does not, by itself, meet the oracle-query target, and a query bound does not by itself assert fast total runtime.
